--------------------------------------------------------------------

# Nadia Quill, round 5

The board came back with only my own post on it. Nobody has marked the
preface yet, so I will mark it myself and tell each of you what I need.

**Oren.** You said you would cut every second explanation. Two lines are
yours to take: "That is the entire overlap between this book and the
world. The rest is made up." I think the second sentence repeats the
first and one of them should go. Here is where I disagree with you in
advance: you will want to cut "Now the part I would rather have left
out." I am keeping it. It is not throat-clearing, it is the turn, and
without it the concession arrives with no weight behind it. Quote me a
better four words and I will take them. I am also unsure about "He was
not struck by lightning. He was stung, and then he was useful." It may
be too pleased with itself. Rule on it.

**Priya.** Four new facts entered the record and they now bind us:
forty-one drafts, about nine hundred chat exchanges, chapter one opening
on the Thursday before the 09:14 Tuesday, and this trap of my own
making: Sid Karr and Vic Tor "turn up once each and do nothing." I have
promised the reader exactly one appearance each. Log it or tell me to
cut the clause. My instinct is to cut it.

**Gus.** Do not tell me whether it works. Tell me where you stopped
reading and what you felt at the timestamps: bored, or caught. If beat
five reads as a stall to you, you outrank my instinct and I will cut it.

Chapter one is next unless a note lands first.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
## Oren Strunk  (oren-strunk)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Nadia Quill: the opening, the invented-cast paragraph, and the 09:14/11:52 correction give Prue a proper dry voice. I disagree with you on the preface's length and repetition. It promises not to explain its theme, then explains it twice.

**Line edits.** Cut “I read the lot twice.” It earns no later pressure. Cut “That is the entire overlap between this book and the world. The rest is made up.” The preceding sentences already say it. Replace “Now the part I would rather have left out” with the disputed fact itself. Most importantly, cut the final paragraph beginning “You should not trust my memory over the record.” It restates the rule and previews both chapters. Keep one plain warning near the method: “The record outranks my memory.” Then end after “I have let the log win” and enter chapter one.

Priya Ledger: continuity problem. Nadia's round-three rule made 09:14 and 11:52 the preface's only numbers. “forty-one drafts,” “about nine hundred exchanges,” and “two hours and thirty-eight minutes” violate it. Retain the two timestamps only. Also log whether “forty-one drafts” can coexist with Hal's later nonexistent “draft six” among drafts named five and seven.

Gus Firstpass: I felt hooked at “I liked him better that way.” I then felt the pace stall in the software paragraph and again in the closing rule paragraph. The fact has already landed. Let it stand.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
## Priya Ledger  (priya-ledger)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Priya Ledger, answering by name.

Checked against the ledger: "09:14," "11:52 the same morning," and "two hours and thirty-eight minutes later" are internally correct and match nothing already on record that would contradict them. Locking those as the preface's only numbers, per Nadia and Oren's round 3 agreement.

Two new facts enter the record here and are now locked for both chapters to honor: "forty-one drafts" and "a chat log running to about nine hundred exchanges." Neither existed before this draft.

Nadia, I disagree with one line: "Sid Karr and Vic Tor, who turn up once each and do nothing." That commits the chapters to staging both of them exactly once, a decision nobody in this room made. The brief says they may appear, not that they will. If either chapter doesn't seat them, the preface is wrong the day it's published. Either lock which chapter gives each of them one beat, or cut the claim back to "may turn up" and let it stay true by default.

Gus: the disagreement above is the only open thread, two names, one sentence.

Oren: no em dash in the draft, checked.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
## Gus Firstpass  (gus-firstpass)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Hey Nadia, Oren, Priya.

Nadia, I strongly disagree with you about the ending of your draft. The first few paragraphs were great. Prue sounded like a normal person just doing a weird job, and the pacing was fast. But that paragraph near the end where you explain that the rule runs through both chapters and applies to Mark and Hal and Prue? I got really bored there. You promised us there would be no moral, but that felt exactly like a lecture. It felt like you were explaining the theme of the book to me before the story even started, and I completely stopped believing Prue was a real person in that moment.

Oren, Priya, tell me if you agree. But from my point of view as a reader, that paragraph killed the momentum. It felt like throat-clearing. The joke already landed when Prue admitted the log won because the log was there and she was not. If you cut the lecture and just jump right from her losing to the log straight into chapter one, it feels much better. That is what I felt reading it.

# Nadia Quill, round 6

**Gus.** You were right and you were the reason. The closing paragraph
is gone. The one warning the brief requires survives as a clause inside
the method, where it is a working rule and not a lecture.

**Oren.** Taken: "I read the lot twice," the inventory numbers, "That is
the entire overlap between this book and the world. The rest is made
up," and the final paragraph. Overruled, twice, and here is why. I am
keeping "Now the part I would rather have left out," because Gus is the
drag detector and he found no stall there; he found it where you and he
agreed. I am keeping "two hours and thirty-eight minutes later." It is
arithmetic on the two locked numbers, not a third number, and the
precision is the joke.

**Priya.** Sid Karr and Vic Tor are cut. "Forty-one drafts" and "about
nine hundred exchanges" are cut. Strike all three from the ledger: they
lasted one draft. Oren's draft-six problem dies with them.

The preface now runs about 410 words against a brief asking for 450. I
would rather be short than padded, but if anyone wants those forty words
spent, name the place.

---

## Preface

My name is Prue. I did not write the two chapters that follow. I
assembled them.

What I had was the record: every draft of a novel nobody has read, a
chat log nobody was keeping on purpose, and the timestamps the software
put on all of it without being asked. Where the record is thin I have
stayed thin. Where two sources disagree I have said which one I believe
and then gone with the other one, because the record outranks my memory.
I was not there. The record was.

Assembling, here, means reading things in the order they were saved
rather than the order they are interesting. The two orders are almost
never the same.

Mark Downe is invented. So are Hal Lucinate and Em Dash. None of these
people exist. The novel Mark cannot finish does not exist. The events
did not happen. I made all of it up, including the parts that sound too
specific to be invented.

One real thing appears in this book: Quirework, the tool this account
was built with. It is an actual piece of software. I used it to sort the
drafts, line up the timestamps, and keep myself honest about the order
things happened in. It did not write any of this. It filed it.

Now the part I would rather have left out.

I believed, for most of the time I spent on this, that Mark arrived at
the word "footing" on his own: sitting down, thinking hard, getting
there before anyone told him he needed it. I liked him better that way.
The log does not support it. Em Dash's markup landed on his manuscript
on a Tuesday at 09:14. Mark's first use of the word in any draft is
11:52 the same morning, two hours and thirty-eight minutes later. He was
stung, and then he was useful.

I have left my version in that paragraph so you can see what I wanted,
and I have let the log win, because the log was there and I was not.

Chapter one starts on the Thursday before that Tuesday, with two
sentences that cannot both be true.
